                    ### Question
                    A 12-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with a 2-day history of fever and generalized weakness. She says that her son was involved in a school fight with some other kids 4 days ago and sustained minor injuries to the face. He was otherwise well, until this morning, when he complained of pain in his right eye. Physical examination reveals periorbital erythema and edema of the right eye, along with ophthalmoplegia and proptosis. Which of the following findings will most likely be present in this patient on the affected side as a sequela of his current condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Anesthesia along the CN V3 distribution
opb. Decreased vision with sparing of the optic disc
opc. Monocular diplopia
opd. Intact sympathetic innervation to the pupil, but not parasympathetic innervation
ope. Absent blink reflex

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 12-year-old boy presents with fever, weakness, periorbital erythema, edema, ophthalmoplegia, and proptosis, suggesting a possible orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus involvement due to recent facial trauma. In cases of orbital cellulitis, cranial nerve involvement can lead to sensory deficits. The most likely sequela on the affected side is anesthesia along the CN V3 distribution, as this nerve is responsible for sensation in the lower face and can be affected by inflammation or compression in the orbital region. Other options, such as decreased vision, monocular diplopia, and absent blink reflex, may occur but are less directly supported by the clinical presentation and consensus on the sequelae of orbital cellulitis. Therefore, the best-supported finding is anesthesia along the CN V3 distribution.
